extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, patent/trademark judges, and lawyers (Korea)
extracted.subtask_description: Judicial criteria and procedural guidance for (1) the "freely usable technology" defense in patent scope/infringement confirmation trials and (2) assessment of intrinsic and acquired distinctiveness, functionality, and likelihood of confusion for three-dimensional trademarks in Korean litigation. Summarizes how courts extract and compare compositional elements, specify accused inventions by claim, and weigh evidence such as surveys and market use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freely usable technology defense (general character)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that does not deny the existence of the patent right but requires determining whether the accused invention falls under the public domain (freely usable technology) that the patent's monopolistic right cannot reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be raised before or after comparison with the patented invention; does not deny patent existence but may render enforcement ineffective for that accused invention. Courts have treated it variously (prior art exclusion view, abuse of right view, freely usable technology defense view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject of obviousness determination (whole composition view)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patented invention is composed of many elements, the subject of the obviousness determination is the technological idea that is the organic combination of each compositional element — not each individual element separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By parity, the same applies to the accused invention: the entire accused invention (its unified composition) must be considered in obviousness determinations; dissolving the unity of compositional elements or excluding portions is not allowed (cites Korean Supreme Court decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for request for judgment and determination of trial subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The party requesting judgment must file a request for judgment form stating the purpose and reasons (Article 140(1) Korean Patent Act); the subject of the trial is determined by those entries, not independently by KITAB or court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim and each accused invention become distinct subjects of the trial; entries in the request define the trial scope. The confirmation trial resembles a lawsuit seeking to confirm the right to prohibit and damages arising from infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of determinations: comparison vs. defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses (including freely usable technology) are typically considered after the 'facts of the reasons for request' are acknowledged — i.e., after comparing accused invention to the patented invention to establish that the accused invention incorporates the patented composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some authority allows addressing the freely usable technology defense before detailed comparisons, as a matter of litigation procedure defenses follow fact-acknowledgement. Internal Comparison (comparing equivalent compositional elements) is distinct from comparison of specifics; internal comparison need not always precede the defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for proving freely usable technology (focus on equivalent elements and prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show the accused invention is freely usable technology, it is sufficient to show that the compositional elements of the accused invention that are equivalent to compositional elements of the patented invention are either entirely composed of prior art or can be easily derived from the prior art by a PHOSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defense concerns whether the accused invention is in the realm of technology outside the reach of the patent right, not a blanket finding of non-novelty/non-obviousness for the entire accused invention. Additional compositional elements outside the equivalent ones need not be shown to be prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraction and Internal Comparison of equivalent compositional elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing accused and patented inventions, the court may extract only the compositional elements of the accused invention that are equivalent to the patented invention's elements and compare those elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extraction is a selective comparison for determination purposes and does not mean the court treats the accused invention as merely a collection of those elements. The same method is used in freely usable technology determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim determination when multiple claims exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patented invention has multiple claims, the composition of the accused invention that is the object of the freely usable technology determination differs for each claim; results may differ claim-by-claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations must be made for each relationship between each individual claim and the accused invention (e.g., 'for the relationship between the accused invention and Claim 1, the accused invention is freely usable technology').

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying accused invention by claim (per-claim specification method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff or the requester should be allowed to specify only the compositional elements to be compared to each claim when there are one or more accused inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting per-claim specification avoids dismissal when extraneous/mistakenly specified elements (e.g., C") would otherwise render the accused invention unspecified or incorrectly implemented. Example: Claim1 = A+B → specify A'+B'; Claim2 = A+B+C → specify A'+B'+C'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of multiple accused inventions in a single confirmation trial
rubrics_metrics.description: It is suggested that multiple accused inventions be allowed in a single trial to confirm the scope of a patent; merging requests for convenience essentially conducts multiple trials concurrently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merging requests does not require combining per-claim specifics into one specification; plaintiff may still specify accused inventions by claim even if trials are merged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of defining accused invention composition narrowly for freely usable technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining the accused invention's composition only to those elements that are equivalent to the patented invention aligns better with the purpose of the freely usable technology defense than defining the accused invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrower definition focuses the inquiry on relevant equivalences and prior art-derived elements rather than on extraneous additional features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic distinctiveness of three-dimensional trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-dimensional product shape can have intrinsic distinctiveness, but because product shapes are often created for functional/aesthetic reasons rather than source identification, distinctiveness of three-dimensional marks should be acknowledged in a limited scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical reluctance to register product shapes exists; courts assess whether the shape (e.g., pill shape + color) goes beyond a general product form and has source-identifying characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired distinctiveness (secondary meaning) for three-dimensional marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Even marks lacking intrinsic distinctiveness (e.g., those falling under Article 6(1)(iii)) may be registered if consumers have come to prominently recognize the form as indicating a product of a particular source through use before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive consideration of factors such as characteristics of the shape, period/duration of use, sales quantity and market share, duration/size of advertising and promotion, magnitude of competitive use with similar forms, and reputation/credit of the trademark user is required. Interpretation/application should be stringent; three-dimensional product forms accompanied by other marks may still obtain acquired distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality / Article 7(1)(xiii) and Article 6(1)(iii) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Shapes or colors that are indispensable for acquiring the product's function (functionality) or are general forms of the product (e.g., pill shape regulated by Article 6(1)(iii)) lack distinctiveness and are barred from trademark protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the shape/color is a general form used in trade for that product or indispensable for the product's function; if so, trademark registration/effect may be denied as lacking distinctiveness or being functional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity/infringement assessment for three-dimensional trademarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess outer appearance similarity by considering dominant characteristics visible in plane and perspective views, the visibility of differences given product size, and whether the defendant is using shape/color as a mark to indicate source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider relationship between mark and product, the form of the mark used, and consumer behavior (e.g., pills are ultimately viewed after removing packaging). Small edge differences may not be visible given size; evaluate dominant impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of packaging, labeling, and transaction-stage indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Packaging and labels (external and internal) carrying product names, company names, or other trademarks may reduce reliance on shape as the source indicator during the transaction stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, because consumers may handle and take pills out of packaging (and single-item trades occur), the pill's shape and color can still function as a source indicator post-transaction; packaging differences are relevant but not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence (surveys, market data) to establish likelihood of confusion or distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence such as pharmacist surveys, market overlap, sales/advertising data, and media attention can support findings of confusion or acquired distinctiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual survey results showing significant confusion among pharmacists were relied upon to acknowledge likelihood of confusion despite prescription status; use such evidence to demonstrate consumer recognition or confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of consumer group and trade context (prescription medicines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if products are prescription-based and primarily handled by professionals (doctors/pharmacists), likelihood of confusion must be assessed in context; professional handling does not preclude confusion if surveys and market behavior show overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that prescription goods may nonetheless be traded singly among general consumers, have overlapping consumer groups, and be subject to consumer recognition beyond the transaction stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent of user (bad faith imitation) as evidentiary factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the defendant intentionally imitated shape and color to take advantage of the plaintiff's established reputation and quality assurance supports findings of infringement and likelihood of confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at marketing, media interest, timing of launch, and similarity of form to infer intention to free-ride on the plaintiff's distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on the effects/scope of trademark rights (balancing commonality and acquired distinctiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a three-dimensional mark has been used exclusively and acquired distinctiveness, courts evaluate whether the form is nonetheless a general trade form or functionally indispensable; Article 6(1)(iii) may render a registered shape non-distinctive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court application: a blue diamond pill shape can be seen as a general pill form combined with regulated color use; hence registration effects may be curtailed if the form is within commonly adopted pill design.
